READING

**The capacity problem, quantified**

Peak requirement is 18 pallets × 4-day collection cycle = 72 spaces. Current entitlement is 52. Shortfall is 20 spaces. In July 2026 that shortfall sent 18.2 t to the processor, costing GBP 45,136 in lost margin (18,200 kg × GBP 2.48 differential). That figure is the annual cost of the status quo and sets the value of fixing it.

Both courses fix it. HAVERSHOLT gives 104 spaces at Wildern Cross, 32 above requirement. TREGOWAN gives 52 + 30 = 82, 10 above requirement. Neither course is materially better than the other on headroom.

**The compressor liability belongs to both courses, not just HAVERSHOLT**

A critical point that changes the arithmetic: TREGOWAN does not dispose of the Wildern Cross shareholding. Under TREGOWAN, Marged retains her 25% stake and therefore faces 25% of the GBP 260,000 compressor bill = GBP 65,000 within approximately three years regardless. HAVERSHOLT raises that to 50% = GBP 130,000. The incremental compressor cost of choosing HAVERSHOLT over TREGOWAN is therefore GBP 65,000, not GBP 130,000.

**Full capital comparison**

| | HAVERSHOLT | TREGOWAN |
|---|---|---|
| Acquisition | GBP 96,000 | – |
| Compressor share (within ~3 yr) | GBP 130,000 | GBP 65,000 |
| Annual rental + haulage | – | GBP 31,200/yr |
| **Total, year 0–3** | **GBP 226,000** | **GBP 65,000 + GBP 93,600 = GBP 158,600** |

So HAVERSHOLT costs roughly GBP 67,400 more over three years — but it produces an owned asset (50% of a store whose replacement value is GBP 260,000+) while TREGOWAN produces nothing durable.

Annual saving of HAVERSHOLT over TREGOWAN: GBP 31,200.
Net extra capital cost: GBP 96,000 purchase + GBP 65,000 extra compressor = GBP 161,000.
Simple payback: GBP 161,000 ÷ GBP 31,200 ≈ **5.2 years**, after which HAVERSHOLT is cheaper every year, with a retained asset.

**Capital feasibility**

Available capital: GBP 140,000.
HAVERSHOLT draws GBP 96,000 immediately, leaving GBP 44,000.
The compressor is "within three years," so say by 2029. The gap between the GBP 44,000 left and the GBP 130,000 compressor bill is GBP 86,000 — approximately GBP 29,000 per year that must come from trading or borrowing. Solving the chilling problem recovers roughly GBP 45,136 per peak season immediately; the first year's saving alone covers more than half that annual gap. This is tight but workable, and it is the kind of debt that services itself.

Under TREGOWAN, GBP 140,000 is intact, but the GBP 65,000 compressor still falls due. That leaves roughly GBP 75,000 in hand — comfortable, but it buys nothing.

**The Ardwick pre-emption is not a real cost**

If Ardwick matches within 30 days, Marged does not spend GBP 96,000 and simply pursues TREGOWAN. She is no worse off than today. The pre-emption is a free option for her: she gets HAVERSHOLT or she gets the status quo — not a penalty.

**The buyer handling query is material**

Ilsington is 14 miles away. Soft fruit that is already been picked, packed and chilled must be loaded, driven, handled at a remote site, and collected — all of which adds risk of bruising, temperature excursion and delay. The buyer has already flagged this. In premium soft fruit, buyer relationships and product quality are the business. TREGOWAN carries this risk permanently and at growing cost if the buyer reduces the premium, demands a price concession or switches suppliers. The potential value at stake — GBP 3.10/kg across the full crop — is far larger than GBP 31,200/year. This risk cannot be fully quantified but it is directionally decisive.

**Governance**

At 50%, Marged has equal votes with Ardwick on every future decision: compressor replacement timing, capex approach, access rules, store management. At 25% she has none of that; Ardwick at 75% can run the store as it pleases. When the compressor conversation arrives, that distinction will be felt.

**Decision**

HAVERSHOLT costs more in the near term and demands careful cash management. It recovers the capital through annual savings by year five, retains a durable asset, eliminates the buyer-handling risk that TREGOWAN permanently carries, and gives Marged a governing voice at Wildern Cross. TREGOWAN is operationally cheaper in years one to five but produces no asset, worsens the commercial position with the buyer, and locks in recurring cost for as long as it is used.

---

READING
  Both courses solve the 20-space capacity shortfall. The compressor liability at 25% (GBP 65,000) falls under TREGOWAN too, so the true incremental capital cost of HAVERSHOLT is GBP 161,000, recovering at GBP 31,200/year (5.2-year payback) plus a retained asset. Capital is stretched but the first season's recovered margin (≈ GBP 45,000) services most of the gap. The Ardwick pre-emption is costless to trigger — if Ardwick matches, TREGOWAN is still available. What tips it clearly is the buyer's handling query: TREGOWAN carries a permanent soft-fruit quality and commercial-relationship risk that HAVERSHOLT eliminates entirely.

CALL
  HAVERSHOLT

GROUNDS
  The buyer has already queried extra handling at a remote site, a quality and commercial-relationship risk that TREGOWAN carries permanently and that HAVERSHOLT eliminates, while the 5-year capital payback and retained asset make HAVERSHOLT the better long-run position even after correcting for the compressor liability that arises under both courses.
